facts.raw_span: recurrent abdominal pain and syncope after drinking alcohol
symptoms persisting for 2 years but worsening on admission
symptoms usually occurred 6-20 hours after alcohol ingestion and lasted 5-10 minutes
syncope occurred only after large alcohol intake
hypertension diagnosed 3 months prior
smoking and alcohol overconsumption (250g/week) for about 20 years
No specific physical examination findings were documented in the case report
High-sensitivity troponin I: 0.01 ng/mL (normal)
Serum potassium: 4.6 mEq/L (normal)
High-degree atrioventricular block and premature ventricular contractions
ST segments elevated 4-6 mm in leads II, III and aVF, with ST depression in leads V2-V6
10% stenosis in proximal left anterior descending artery (LAD) and right coronary artery (RCA)

concepts.why: The patient's long history of excessive alcohol consumption and the presence of high-degree atrioventricular block and premature ventricular contractions, as well as ST segment elevations, suggest alcoholic cardiomyopathy as a possible diagnosis.

The ECG findings of high-degree atrioventricular block, premature ventricular contractions, and ST segment elevations could be indicative of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, although the patient's history of alcohol abuse and lack of specific physical examination findings make this less likely.

The presence of ST segment elevations and premature ventricular contractions, along with the coronary angiography results showing 10% stenosis in the proximal LAD and RCA, suggest coronary artery disease as a possible diagnosis, although the stenosis is relatively mild.

The patient's symptoms of syncope and the ECG findings of premature ventricular contractions and ST segment elevations could be indicative of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, although this diagnosis would require further evaluation and confirmation.

The patient's history of excessive alcohol consumption and the temporal relationship between alcohol ingestion and symptoms suggest that alcohol-induced arrhythmias could be a contributing factor to the patient's condition.

rationales.F04: Syncope occurring only after large alcohol intake further supports the connection to alcohol consumption, making Alcoholic Cardiomyopathy and Alcohol-Induced Arrhythmias more likely.
rationales.F06: Long-term smoking and alcohol overconsumption are significant risk factors for Alcoholic Cardiomyopathy, Coronary Artery Disease, and Alcohol-Induced Arrhythmias, making these conditions more probable.
rationales.F10: The presence of high-degree atrioventricular block and premature ventricular contractions is indicative of arrhythmias, which can be associated with Alcoholic Cardiomyopathy, Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy, and Alcohol-Induced Arrhythmias.
rationales.F12: The minimal stenosis found in the coronary arteries reduces the likelihood of Coronary Artery Disease being the primary cause, thus ruling it out and also decreasing the likelihood of Alcoholic Cardiomyopathy, which can sometimes present with coronary artery disease.
